To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a strain of Fusarium solani has been isolated that is able to utilize benzonitrile, a nitrile, as a sole source of carbon, nitrogen and energy.

the nitriles of benzonitriles, 4-hydroxybenzonitrile, 3,4- dihydroxybenzonitriles, and phenylacetonitriles, are degraded by a nitrilase, and that this nitrilase is composed of eight identical subunits, each with a molecular weight of 76 000.

we have isolated a strain of the fungus that is able to grow on benzonitrile, that the nitrilenitrile is catabolised via benzoate, and that the fungus has an enzyme that is able to convert benzonitrile to benzoate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the degradation of nitriles by the soil fungus Fusarium solanif.
the enzymology of C-N bond cleavage of nitriles by Fusarium solanii.
the enzymology of the biotransformation of aromatic nitrilic compounds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Fusarium solani is a nitrilase-producing fungus, the enzyme having a molecular weight of 620000.
the enzyme is a nitrilase.
this enzyme is the first nitrilase from a eukaryotic organism to be characterized in such detail and the first nitrile-cleaving enzyme to be purified from a fungal source.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the nitrilation process is a common pathway for the degradation of aromatic n-cyano compounds in nature.
we have isolated and purified a nitrilase from Fusarium solani which can degrade benzonitrile and other aromatic nitriles.
Fusarium solani is a very useful organism to study nitrilic compounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified an enzyme in Fusarium solani that is responsible for the cleavage of the C-N bond in nitriles and the formation of the corresponding carboxylate and ammonia.
the enzyme is a nitrilase that catalyzes the hydrolysis of nitrile to carboxylic acid and ammonia.
nitrilase enzymes are not as rare as previously thought.
